newsitem.title: UK: UK firm launches car insurance over the Internet.
newsitem.headline: UK firm launches car insurance over the Internet.

text.p: B.A.T Industries Plc's Eagle Star insurance company on Wednesday launched what it claimed was the world's first car insurance service on the Internet.
UK customers will be able to buy car insurance cover instantaneously from Eagle Star Direct - 24 hours a day. Personal details and payments will be taken whilst the customer is on-line.
The move is likely to mark another step in what promises to be an explosion of business on the Internet in the next few years.

In April, Halifax began selling travel insurance on-line. Guardian Royal Exchange already offers a computer insurance product on the Internet, though payments are still via the ordinary postal network.
Britain's leading supplier of software systems to insurance brokers Misys is also developing software to allow customers to obtain car insurance on the Internet.
Until now, many insurance companies have largely restricted their services to pages of company and product information.
But three quarters of financial services firms in a recent survey conducted by Ernst & Young said that they planned to transact business over the Internet by 1999.
Many will be watching the success of Eagle Star's new product with interest.
Eagle Star said it expects its "cyber insurance" to be a big hit.
Customers fill out a form on screen and get an instant quote. If they decide to take up the quote, they type in their credit or debit card details and the payment is made.
Users can alter the information, such as having another driver insured, to see what difference it makes to the premium.
Prices will be up to 25 percent lower than Eagle Star Direct's telephone-based operations.
"We believe that uncomplicated car insurance, which is easily accessible and inexpensive, will prove very popular", said a spokesman for the company.

"By fully automating the insurance buying process, we are opening up a completely new distribution channel. Whilst some customers will always prefer to buy insurance over the 'phone or via an intermediary, we have recognised the opportunities presented by the huge growth in the Internet's popularity."
Home and travel cover is planned to follow in coming months.
British companies like supermarket chain Tesco already offer an on-line shopping service but in many ways, insurance is even more suited to the Internet.
There are no actual goods involved and policy documentation and payment can be easily transferred.
Problems do exist - the Internet can be slow and question marks remain over security.
Eagle Star, however, said it was confident that its site is secure.
There are some 4.6 million users of the Internet in the UK and around 12 million homes are expected to be connected by the year 2000.
One recent report predicted that annual trade over the Internet will reach $600 billion by the turn of the century.
-- Simon Cowell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7721
